schools.summary: Gill: Eliphaz, probably the senior and most reverenced friend, speaks first when Job has done cursing his day; he 'answered' by taking occasion from Job's passionate words, and 'said' nothing of comfort but reproached him as wicked and hypocritical.

Clarke: after seven days' awed silence Eliphaz forgets he came as a comforter and turns censor, aiming to strip Job of the testimony of his conscience by insinuating that upright ways would not have ended in such distress.
Henry: Eliphaz begins with modesty and tenderness toward one in grief, yet will pass from a just reproof of Job's impatience to an unjust charge of hypocrisy, doing Satan's work unawares.
Gill: Eliphaz speaks for all three, who had consulted and settled a plan of attack; his words hover between doubt and resolve, fearing to grieve a man already bowed down yet determined to speak.

Henry: a double note of modesty ('we will commune,' begging leave only to assay, as discourses go under the title of essays) and tenderness, afraid to add affliction to the afflicted, joined to assurance that God's honour must be vindicated.

Clarke calls it a plausible and sincere beginning: many reproofs must come, yet since Job has spoken words injurious to his Maker, who can forbear? Wesley notes the same modesty and that Eliphaz is provoked by such words from such a man.

Keil and Delitzsch parse the paratactic interrogation ('wilt thou, if we speak, feel it unbearable?') and weigh an Aramaic spelling of the verb; Ellicott would render 'Has one ever assayed?' and sets Job's honour from Job 29:9-10, noting the friends' keynote that suffering proves wickedness.

Gill reads the 'behold' as a note of admiration and attention: this great and good man had condescended to teach many, apt and able in things natural, civil, and religious, instructing household, neighbours, and friends.
Clarke: Job had counselled many in distress with advice effectual to their relief, strengthening the weak hands and feeble knees by word and example.

Henry dwells warmly on Job's ministry (the tongue of the learned, a word in season, borrowed from Isa. 35:3-4) but weighs why Eliphaz recalls it: preface to reproof, ground for expecting comfort, pity, or 'physician, heal thyself' (Rom. 2:21).

Ellicott hears a conspicuous want of feeling, Eliphaz almost rejoicing that the great helper now needs help; Keil and Delitzsch keep the rendering of Job's past kindness, poised to be turned against him.

debates.question: Does Eliphaz recall Job's past ministry in tenderness or in reproach?

sides.position: as a kindly preface, pity, or ground for expecting comfort
with a want of feeling, almost rejoicing that the helper now needs help

schools.summary: Gill unfolds 'him that was falling' as 'stumbling' three ways: stumbling at God's providence toward the afflicted righteous, stumbling from religion under persecution, or sinking under affliction; Job's seasonable words upheld all such (the Targum: falling into sin).

Henry reads the paired clauses as spiritual charity: strengthening weak hands for warfare and feeble knees for the journey, in the language of Isa. 35:3-4; a good word well spoken does more good than we think.
Wesley glosses the 'feeble knees' as the weak-hearted, fainting under their trials.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the stumbling turned to thy words, and the sinking knees thou hast strengthened,' the picture set to be turned against Job in the next verse.

themes: the healer who cannot heal himself

schools.summary: Gill: the same trial that struck those Job comforted has now reached him, and he faints and sinks impatiently, contrary to his own counsel, so Eliphaz concludes he was upright only in show; he rejects Bolducius's 'God cometh unto thee.'

Clarke frames it as a demand for consistency: now prove the efficacy of thy own principles; since thou faintest, either thou didst pretend to what thou hadst not, or thou failest to use what thou taughtest.

Henry catches the double unfairness: too light of the affliction ('it toucheth thee,' Satan's own word, Job 1:11; 2:5) and too much of the resentment ('thou ravest'), when the distressed deserve grains of allowance.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'now it cometh to thee, thou art grieved; now it toucheth thee, thou despondest,' the 'now' answering the many Job once raised.

themes: faint in the day of adversity
grains of allowance for the distressed

schools.summary: Ellicott lays out the two construals: either Job's piety should be his confidence and ground of hope, or his reverence and integrity are shown worthless since he faints as soon as adversity touches him; the drift is much the same.

Gill expounds 'thy fear' as the grace of the fear of God, no slavish dread but a reverential affection that hates sin and is joined with faith and holiness, which Job professed; Eliphaz asks where it now appears.
Clarke prefers Coverdale's 'Where is now thy fear of God, thy steadfastness, thy patience?'; Wesley makes the sting plain, that Job's carriage shows his religion to have been but talk and appearance.

Henry names this the graver charge and refuses it: Eliphaz upbraids Job's whole profession as a sham, the very aim of Satan; and though Prov. 24:10 says the fainting man's strength is small, a character is not to be judged from a single act.

debates.question: How is the question of v.6 to be construed?

sides.position: Job's piety should be his confidence and sufficient ground of hope
Job's fear and integrity are exposed as hollow by his fainting

themes: the fear of God as grace
Satan's aim to prove Job a hypocrite

schools.summary: Gill weighs 'perished': not eternal ruin (the innocent never so perish) nor bodily death (the innocent do die); the 'innocent' is the truly gracious man, guilty of no notorious crime.

Ellicott calls it the friends' great half-truth, meant either to insinuate secret sin or, more graciously, to ground the innocent man's hope, since God fails none who trust him though he may try them; Keil and Delitzsch render the questions as indignant exclamations.

Henry distinguishes senses: true of eternal destruction (the man of sin the son of perdition, 2 Thess. 2:3), but false of temporal calamity (Eccl. 9:2; Isa. 57:1), citing Abel, Lot, and Jacob 'ready to perish' (Deut. 26:5).
Clarke reads an appeal to memory that could reassure the innocent; Wesley hears a veiled indictment, that Job must be guilty of some secret crime now found out, 'cut off' by divine vengeance.

debates.question: What is Eliphaz's drift in appealing to who ever perished innocent?

sides.position: a veiled insinuation that Job is secretly guilty
a ground of hope, since the truly innocent are not finally allowed to perish

debates.question: Does 'perish / cut off' mean eternal ruin or temporal calamity?

sides.position: eternal destruction, in which sense the maxim is true but ill applied to Job
temporal calamity, in which sense it is false, for the righteous also perish

schools.summary: Gill: Eliphaz proves from his own experience that the wicked are destroyed, insinuating that Job's ruin marks him one of them.

Clarke heaps up the sowing/reaping parallels (Prov. 22:8; Gal. 6:7-8; Hos. 10:13, almost Eliphaz's words; Aeschylus), a universal law of nature; Wesley reads the ploughers as designed, deliberate sinners reaping the just punishment of their iniquity.
Henry: the busy, politic sinners take pains in sin and reap corruption (Gal. 6:8), or, as wrong done to others, are paid in their own coin (2 Thess. 1:6; Isa. 33:1).
Ellicott confirms the web of allusion (Gal. 6:7-8; the strange expression of Isa. 5:18).

themes: the law of sowing and reaping
a general truth misapplied to Job

schools.summary: Gill hears an allusion to corn blasted by the east wind or mildew: as suddenly as grain withers, the wicked perish when God blows a blast on their persons, substance, and families.

Clarke: as the parching east wind destroys vegetation, so the wicked perish under God's indignation; Wesley reads 'of his nostrils' as God's anger, a secret but mighty judgment blowing them away like chaff.

Henry distinguishes 'perish' (destroyed utterly) from 'consumed' (destroyed by degrees), by God's wrath (Isa. 30:33; Ps. 90:11) and his word (2 Thess. 2:8), and suspects Eliphaz glances at the wind that killed Job's children (Luke 13:2).

outliers.note: Suspects that in speaking of destruction by a blast of wind Eliphaz cruelly alludes to the wind that blew down the house upon Job's children, as though they were sinners above others (the insinuation rebuked in Luke 13:2).

schools.summary: Gill reports Aben Ezra (the lion is God), R. Moses and R. Jonah (literal beasts of prey as God's judgment), and his own preference with Jarchi and Ben Gersom for tyrannical kings and princes likened to lions.

Clarke reads all the lions as tyrannous rulers whom God's justice casts down, their whelps scattered; Wesley agrees they are powerful tyrants (Ezek. 32:2), and suspects Eliphaz secretly accuses Job or his children of oppression.

Henry develops the several Hebrew names for lion as figures of proud oppressors, whose destruction he traces limb by limb (teeth broken, Ps. 3:7), sensing a personal thrust at Job the great man of the east.

debates.question: Whom or what does the lion represent?

sides.position: God himself, who tears the wicked in wrath
literal beasts of prey sent as God's judgment
holders: R. Moses and R. Jonah (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: tyrannical kings and oppressors

themes: a veiled charge against Job's house

schools.summary: Gill renders 'the stout lion' perishing not for want of finding prey but of keeping it, taken from him; God strips oppressors of their spoil; he notes and rejects the Septuagint's 'ant-lion,' though Strabo and Aelian tell of lions called ants.

Clarke sets out the five Hebrew words for lion (aryeh, shachal, kephir, layish, labi) with their roots and qualities, granting they came to designate the beast simply; Wesley reads the whelps 'scattered,' hunting and finding no prey.
Ellicott notes the five words show how common and various lions were in Job's country, and that wickedness joined with strength equally fails to prosper.

outliers.note: Records the Septuagint's rendering 'ant-lion' (with Isidore's description and the reports of Strabo and Aelian about lions called ants in Arabia and Babylon), only to reject it as the animal here meant.

schools.summary: Gill defends the vision's genuineness against those calling it a fiction or diabolical: nothing in manner or matter is unworthy of divine revelation, Eliphaz was a good if mistaken man, and Job never charges him with inventing it; its burden is God's holiness and man's frailty.

Henry: the message was real and would have served to reprove Job's murmuring had Eliphaz kept its purport; it came secretly, by stealth, and only 'a little' was received, for the best know but little of God (1 Cor. 13:12).

Clarke: Eliphaz professes a vision to give himself authority, then misapplies its doctrine, rendering (with Good) 'a whisper along with it'; Wesley reads a 'word' from God stolen by stealth, spoken low as to the prophets, only partly perceived.

Ellicott: 'secretly brought' is literally 'was stolen for me' (as Joseph, Gen. 40:15), and 'a little' a rare word recurring only in Job 26:14; Eliphaz rises into highly poetical language (versified by Byron).

debates.question: Is Eliphaz's vision a genuine divine revelation?

sides.position: a true revelation from God, orthodox in matter though misapplied
a mere fiction of Eliphaz, or even a diabolical vision

schools.summary: Gill takes Eliphaz to have been meditating on divine things when the revelation came, God's usual way of speaking in former times, by vision of day or night.

Wesley distinguishes vision from dream (God speaks in dreams asleep, in visions awake), Eliphaz being awake in the dead of night; Clarke (with Good and Hervey) exalts the passage as beyond rival in poetry for its midnight terror.

Ellicott grounds night-vision revelation in Genesis and Daniel, noting 'thoughts' recurs only in Job 20:2 and the 'deep sleep' (tardemah) recalls Gen. 2:21; 15:12 and Job 33:15; Keil and Delitzsch carry the flow from sleep into trembling.
Gill: not dread of mind only but bodily trembling, as befell Abraham, Moses, Daniel, and Zechariah at unusual appearances of God, springing from human frailty, guilt, and a sense of God's majesty.
Henry reads the terror as God humbling the man he means to honour: seized with trembling before he heard or saw anything, made ready for a divine visit, for God will have us serve him with holy fear.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake,' the shudder running through the whole frame.

themes: the seer unmanned before the message

schools.summary: Gill lays out the choices: some and the Targum take the 'spirit' for a stormy wind (as Elijah felt, or Job's whirlwind), but he prefers with Jarchi an angel, an immaterial spirit in human form, passing and repassing.
Wesley: an angel in visible shape, else Eliphaz could not have discerned it, the hair standing up from the horror of so terrible a presence.
Ellicott resists literalism: a spirit can be manifested only to the spirit, and 'seeing a spirit' is absurd; but the inner perception may grow so vivid as to seem an outward manifestation.

Henry holds the apparition real, not a dream, an image that passed and repassed and stood still, yet indistinct, producing consternation and hair on end, for every express from heaven is terrible to sinful man.

debates.question: What was the 'spirit' that passed before Eliphaz?

sides.position: a wind or stormy blast
an angel in visible, human form
an inward spiritual perception risen to the vividness of sight, not seen by the bodily eye

themes: a spirit passed before my face
the horror of a heavenly presence

schools.summary: Gill: the spirit, before going to and fro, now stands still over against Eliphaz as one with something to say, standing before him while it speaks that he might take notice.

Wesley reads each clause: the spirit makes a stand to speak, the form seen only as a confused resemblance, then silence (its motion stilled, all hushed, his own breath held), the Hebrew running 'silence and a voice I heard.'
Henry dwells on the solemn pause before the message, a still small voice (recalling the LORD to Elijah), the form left indistinct because conscience, not curiosity, was to be served.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the rendering, the syntax enacting the suspense of the halted, unreadable form and the voice out of silence.
Gill doubts the comparative 'more just than God' (a truth needing no vision) and leans to 'just before God,' that no man is righteous in God's sight.

Clarke renders 'justified before God... pure before his Maker,' the work all God's through atonement and the Spirit, yet denies the words prove none can be justified, for God justifies the ungodly; Wesley presses enosh and geber, that faulting God's law or providence makes one more just than one's Maker.

Henry weighs whether Eliphaz proves Job's afflictions a mark of wickedness or only reproves his murmuring, inclining to the milder sense, but holds it impious for the clay to think itself purer than the potter.
Ellicott calls it the friends' orthodox but inadequate refrain, raising Job's dilemma of God's justice; 'mortal' is properly weak, frail man, and even the strong man cannot be purer than his Maker.

debates.question: How should the question be rendered and construed?

sides.position: comparative: 'more just / more pure than God,' an absurd insolence
'just / justified before God,' that no man is righteous in God's sight

debates.question: What is Eliphaz's aim in the question?

sides.position: to prove Job's afflictions a certain mark of wickedness
only to reprove Job's murmuring and presumption

outliers.note: Adds that the spectre's utterance, whether from heaven or hell, 'shows and rankles a wound, without providing a cure' — orthodox as far as it goes, but no gospel remedy for the sin it exposes.

themes: shall mortal man be more just than God
just before God versus more just than God

schools.summary: Gill takes the oracle to run to the chapter's end and 'his servants' to mean the angels (not prophets or righteous men), in whom God places no such trust as creatures place in one another.

Clarke refers it to the fallen angels who kept not their first estate, surveying the renderings (Vulgate 'perverseness,' Syriac 'amazement,' French 'light,' Montanus 'exultation,' Coverdale 'proud disobedience'); Wesley likewise takes the folly to be the sin of the angels who fell.

Henry turns it on the creaturely limits of even unfallen angels: God needs them not, charges them with folly and imperfection (not iniquity), some inferring the angelic nature so mutable that grace must confirm it.
Ellicott keeps the statement general ('putteth,' 'chargeth,' repeated in Job 15:15); Keil and Delitzsch fix the particle governing v.19 as 'how much more' after a positive clause (2 Sam. 16:11).

debates.question: What is the 'folly' charged on the angels?

sides.position: the sin of the angels who fell from their first estate
the finiteness and imperfection of even the holy angels compared with God

schools.summary: Gill: the house of clay is not the grave (against the Targum) but the body in which the soul dwells, showing the soul's excellency and separability; called clay for its dusty origin and frailty (Epictetus, 'clay elegantly wrought').

Keil and Delitzsch ground it in Gen. 2:7 and 3:19 and take 'before the moth' as 'in the presence of,' rejecting 'sooner than a moth'; Ellicott sees a glance at the brick-making of Gen. 11:3, man so frail the moth destroys him.

Clarke, reading 'how much more,' says the slightest accident kills ('a fly, a grape-stone, or a hair'); Wesley contrasts the free angelic spirits with man's mortal body of clay, its foundation in the dust, crushed by so contemptible a thing as a moth.
Henry meditates on man's meanness: the soul housed in a cottage of clay founded in dust, sinking by its own weight, crushed like a moth between the fingers (Hos. 5:12-14).

debates.question: How is 'crushed before the moth' to be taken?

sides.position: sooner or more easily than a moth is itself crushed
holders: Hahn (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: even the moth destroys them; 'before' = in the presence of

themes: how much more than the angels

schools.summary: Gill: the dwellers in clay are always exposed to death, life but the space of a day; all men begin to die the day they begin to live, the wise man naming no interval between birth and death (Eccl. 3:2; Ps. 39:5).

Clarke: in almost every moment one is born and one dies; 'perish for ever' as passing by, mouldering, soon forgotten (Isa. 57:1); Wesley reads a continual sinking toward death, and 'without regarding it' as the world's strange carelessness.
Henry unfolds the daily wasting, death working like a mole digging our grave, life but from morning to evening, birth and death the sunrise and sunset of the same day.
Keil and Delitzsch render them broken in pieces from morning to evening, perishing unregarded for ever; Ellicott notes the continual, unceasing process that none regardeth.

outliers.note: Notes the kinship with Isa. 57:1 and raises, then leaves open, whether Isaiah borrowed from Job — which would require proving the book the earlier, never yet done.

schools.summary: Gill takes 'their excellency' for the soul departing at death with every faculty and endowment, or (reading 'with them') for wealth and honour uncarried to the grave, and reports a reference to the lost image of God.
Keil and Delitzsch render a wholly different image: not 'excellency' but the tent-cord torn away, the body a tent that collapses when its cord is plucked up.

Clarke reads the excellency as beauty, strength, eloquence, and gifts plucked up by the roots, and 'without wisdom' as dying in comparative ignorance, the one saving wisdom being to know God and Jesus Christ; Wesley takes it for birth, riches, and power that perish with the houses of clay.

Henry: in death all excellency passes away, wisdom cannot save, men die for want of wisdom, digging their graves with their own teeth, unheeded, unless grace give the wisdom that lays hold on eternal life.

debates.question: What is 'their excellency which is in them'?

sides.position: the soul, or man's endowments, wealth, and honour
the cord of their tent, plucked up so the tent-body collapses

themes: man abased that God's justice may stand
